transcript: HEADER: Date: 2026-12-07 | Start: 15:30 UTC | Duration: 58m | Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Mark, Sara, David (Atlas Financial)
15:30 Jordan Mills: hey everyone thanks for joining, we'll do an optimize walkthrough today focused on batching and our prefix / K-V cache cost model
15:31 Mark Chen: thanks, we've been seeing token costs spike and latency spikes during peak, so curious how batching + cache helps, and what tradeoffs we need to consider
15:32 Priya Rao: cool. quick agenda — 1) quick recap of your traffic 2) batching basics and sizing 3) prefix/KV cache patterns and hit-rate modeling 4) cost model demo 5) pilot proposal — sound ok?

15:33 David Brooks: yep sounds good. Mark sent over a high-level traffic CSV earlier — mix of short chat queries (~12 tokens) and longer summarization (~400 tokens) — about 1200 QPS at peak, mostly user-facing

15:34 Jordan Mills: perfect. so one big thing is request size distribution — if you have lots of short requests, batching helps but increases tail latency; if long requests, batching can increase throughput without as much latency hit

15:35 Priya Rao: right. also sequence length variance impacts GPU kernel choices and KV cache effectiveness. for prefix caching we look at identical prefixes — e.g., repeated system prompts or instruction templates — which can give high hit rates in chat-like flows
15:37 Sara Lopez: quick q: when you say KV cache do you mean token-level kv cache that persists between requests on the serving nodes or an external cache?

15:37 Priya Rao: good question — two layers. Redwood runtime has in-memory KV cache tied to the model instance for prefix reuse (fast, no network), and we can also configure a shared prefix cache (s3/redis like) for cross-instance reuse — but cross-instance brings network/consistency tradeoffs
15:38 Mark Chen: we care about PII — does prefix cache store raw prompts? we need redaction or encryption

15:38 Jordan Mills: yes security: we can configure redaction rules and envelope keys; data at rest can be encrypted with your KMS and we support audit logs. we'll share SOC2 + network diagram after the call

15:40 Priya Rao: diving into batching — there are two knobs: max batch size and max latency window. e.g., at 1200 QPS with mostly short queries we showed customers go from ~12 tps per GPU to ~200 tokens/sec using batching; but if you increase the latency window too much, p50/p95 degrades

15:42 Priya Rao: demo slide: here's a simulation — 3 scenarios. scenario A: aggressive batching (batch size 64, latency window 50ms) improves throughput and lowers cost per token by ~40% but p95 increases from 110ms to 250ms. scenario B: conservative batching (batch size 8, window 10ms) keeps p95 ~120ms but cost savings only ~10%
15:43 Mark Chen: can you tune batching per route? our API has chat endpoints and a background summarize job — we want different SLOs

15:43 Jordan Mills: yes, route-level policies in Console. you can set different batching profiles per route or tag. we often put user-interactive chat on low-latency profile and background jobs on high-throughput profile

15:45 Priya Rao: now prefix/KV cache. imagine 60% of your requests share a common 40-token system prompt. at 70% cache hit you can avoid re-synthesizing those tokens — cost savings compound with batching. our cost model assumes hit-rate tiers: 0%, 30%, 60%, 90%
15:46 David Brooks: what's realistic hit-rate? our prompts have personalization tokens per user, so full hits may be low

15:46 Priya Rao: often you get partial hits — say prefix up to instruction template hits but user-specific tokens are appended. partial hits still save KV compute. we also estimate effective token reduction: e.g., 60% prefix hit reduces average tokens processed by ~25% depending on distribution

15:48 Jordan Mills: important caveat — KV cache works best when you route to warm instances (sticky sessions) or use a shared warm-cache; for ephemeral instances cold-starts kill hit-rate. Dedicated pools help here
15:49 Sara Lopez: Dedicated vs hosted — we have compliance needs, but latency is biggest for us. How does Dedicated affect cost?

15:50 Priya Rao: Dedicated gives more predictable throughput and warm state. Cost model: dedicated is committed capacity — unit cost per GPU is lower at high utilization. Hosted offers burst and simpler ops but instance churn reduces cache efficiency. We'll show spreadsheet examples

15:51 Priya Rao: demo: open cost spreadsheet — column assumptions: qps, avg tokens in/out, cache hit-rate, batch profile, GPU throughput, price per GPU hour. changing hit-rate from 0 to 60% can reduce monthly token compute cost by ~30-45% depending on batching
15:53 Mark Chen: any hidden tradeoffs like hallucination or model quality impact when reusing KV cache?

15:53 Priya Rao: cache doesn't change model weights; it reuses KV states for prefix tokens. But if you incorrectly reuse a prefix that includes mutable state (like conversation with user-sensitive context) you could leak context. So cache keys must be deterministic and scoped — e.g., per-tenant or per-session

15:55 Jordan Mills: other optimizations: quantization profiles for long-form summarize jobs, dynamic batching thresholds, and pre-warming for known peak windows — Optimize can recommend configs automatically based on traffic traces
15:56 David Brooks: you mentioned automatic recommendations. how confident are those? do you run offline sims?

15:56 Priya Rao: we run simulations on representative traffic and we compute cost/latency curves. the Console shows expected p50/p95 and cost delta. for pilots we also run canary benchmarks on your sample traffic to validate predictions
15:58 Jordan Mills: quick interjection — transcription note: we have a few typos in the slides earlier, Jordan said LLM-serve as LLM-swer so ignore that, ha

16:00 Priya Rao: demo: show pilot config — we suggest a two-week pilot: 1 week A/B with hosted optimized profiles, 1 week dedicated with warm cache if you want to test dedicated ROI. we'll collect p50/p95, cost per 1M tokens, and cache hit-rate metrics
16:02 Mark Chen: what instrumentation do you expose? we need token-level cost attribution and traceability per request

16:03 Jordan Mills: Console exposes per-route token breakdown, per-token latency heatmaps, KV cache hit-rate metrics, and request traces. exports are CSV/JSON and we stream logs to your SIEM if required
16:05 Sara Lopez: network/security again — for dedicated/private mode how is KMS integrated? can we bring our own key (BYOK)?
16:05 Priya Rao: yes, BYOK via your cloud KMS or HSM is supported; audit logs, SSO/SAML for RBAC, and optional VPC peering or on-prem package for air-gapped needs
16:07 David Brooks: pricing ask — can you show an example cost vs quality table? we need to present to finance

16:08 Priya Rao: slide: example table — rows show batch profile + cache hit-rate levels; columns show p50/p95 and cost per million tokens. e.g., conservative batching + 30% hit => p95 140ms, cost -15%. aggressive batching + 60% hit => p95 260ms, cost -47%
16:10 Mark Chen: that p95 of 260ms might be borderline for our UX. can we do hybrid—some routes low-latency, some aggressive?

16:11 Jordan Mills: yes exactly — route-level policies plus fallbacks. we can set a canary: if p95 > X ms then fallback to lower batch size or different region. Redwood supports automatic fallback rules

16:12 Priya Rao: also worth calling out cold-start mitigation — we have warm pools and continuous background keep-alives for chosen models, which minimizes cold KV misses. Dedicated also reduces churn so it's better for cache stability
16:14 Sara Lopez: what's the overhead of shared prefix cache (network ff) vs in-memory per-instance?

16:14 Priya Rao: shared cache adds network latency but increases cross-instance reuse. typical pattern: keep short-latency in-memory cache for session stickiness and use shared prefix cache for global templates. we estimate added latency ~5-15ms depending on region

16:16 Jordan Mills: wrapping to next steps — Jordan will send the cost workbook and SOC2 + network diagram; Priya will schedule the pilot and propose the exact route profiles; Mark will provide sample traffic and redaction rules
16:17 David Brooks: ok sounds good. one more quick question — billing granularity? do you bill per-token or per-request in dedicated?
16:18 Jordan Mills: hosted is primarily per-token with some request-level metrics; dedicated is committed GPU hours plus an overage token charge. we'll outline this in the pricing email
16:20 Mark Chen: great. also please include an example of the billing math for our peak month so finance can see project costs
16:21 Jordan Mills: will do. thanks all. Priya anything to add?

16:22 Priya Rao: just that during the pilot we'll instrument KV hit-rate scenarios — please include typical session churn windows so we can model sticky routing. I'll also include expected p50/p95 dashboards in the pilot report
16:23 Sara Lopez: thanks everyone — we'll review internally and get the traffic CSV to you by Monday
16:24 Jordan Mills: thanks — we'll follow up with the sheets and the pilot proposal. end of call
END: 16:28 UTC
